BACKGROUND

A new interface.
A familiar duty.

IN THIS SECTION

The second editorial stage / Meet Xiao La Meng

JMSC6140 · FINAL PROJECT
THE BIG PICTURE

1. Project Background

AI is becoming a gateway to news. Editorial responsibility must follow the story into every generated answer.

CASE STUDYNew HunanFOCUSXiao La Meng
Read the background and scope

Generative artificial intelligence is evolving from a supporting tool in news production into a direct gateway through which readers access, summarize, and understand news. On August 15, 2026, Hunan Daily launched version 13.0 of the New Hunan app. Its AI assistant, “Xiao La Meng,” offers article summaries, suggested questions, interactive explanations, and related-news recommendations (Hunan Daily & New Hunan, 2026).

In the traditional workflow, reporters gather and write stories, which editors review before publication. However, the AI summaries and instant answers readers encounter reorganize information after the original stories have been published. Even when the source article is accurate, AI may omit eligibility criteria, temporal context, or the scope of data. News organizations therefore need to extend editorial responsibility beyond original reporting to AI-generated news explanations presented to readers, rather than treating an “AI-generated content” disclaimer as a substitute for accuracy safeguards.

This proposal focuses on New Hunan as the site for policy implementation and uses Xiao La Meng as its primary case study. It also draws on publicly reported cases involving other AI information services to examine potential risks. Its goal is to establish an actionable framework that combines news accuracy, source traceability, risk-tiered oversight, and accountability for corrections.

2. Problem Statement

The central purpose of traditional editorial review is to ensure that news content meets the professional standards of a news organization before publication. With the emergence of AI news assistants, however, news information may now pass through two distinct editorial stages.

STAGE 1

Traditional editorial review

  • Reporters gather information and write stories.
  • Editors review facts, sources, and content.
  • The stories are subsequently published.
STAGE 2

AI re-summarization and interpretation

Based on published reporting, AI automatically generates summaries, explanations, and follow-up answers that are delivered directly to users.

Although the second stage draws on previously reviewed journalism, its output is not necessarily accurate. AI may:

  • Omit essential context.
  • Conflate facts from different reports.
  • Turn a statement subject to specific conditions into a generalized claim.

If news organizations only ensure that the original articles have been reviewed, without corresponding quality controls and accountability mechanisms for AI outputs, a new gap in editorial governance may emerge.

When AI systems re-summarize and interpret published news, how can news organizations ensure accuracy and establish clear, operational mechanisms for editorial accountability?
MEET THE NEWS ASSISTANT

3. Xiao La Meng

From a news summarization tool
to an interactive information service.

Our observations of the New Hunan app indicate that Xiao La Meng already supports several AI functions embedded at different stages of the news-reading experience.

Article summaries

An overview, reading time and key takeaways appear before the article.

Observation and limitations

An AI summary appears automatically at the beginning of news articles, providing an overview, an estimated reading time, and key takeaways. Readers may therefore encounter an AI-generated account and interpretation of a story before reading the original article.

Suggested questions

Suggested prompts open a separate conversation—and may move beyond the original story.

Observation and limitations

A feature at the end of an article, “Xiao La Meng Thinks You Might Ask,” suggests several questions. Selecting one opens a separate AI chat interface. These prompts do not necessarily focus directly on the article. For example, beneath a story announcing the official launch of Hunan Daily's Zhimou Trusted GEO service, the system recommended a question about governing AI hallucinations. When selected, Xiao La Meng offered a general discussion of AI governance instead of a direct explanation of the specific story.

Article-based Q&A

Readers can ask about a designated article and continue with follow-up questions.

Observation and limitations

Users may open Xiao La Meng themselves, ask it to explain a particular story, and follow up with additional questions. In our test using the Zhimou Trusted GEO story, the assistant summarized the article, extracted its main points, and answered follow-up questions based on the content. Its capabilities therefore include not only broad topic exploration but also question answering grounded in a designated news report.

Related-news recommendations

Links invite further reading, but do not establish support for every claim.

Observation and limitations

Xiao La Meng also provides related-article recommendations at the end of each response, allowing users to access the original news stories. This offers a pathway for deeper reading and verification. However, the presence of related articles does not mean that each factual claim in an AI answer is directly supported by them. We noticed that some recommended stories had very similar titles. The relevance and diversity of recommendations, and their correspondence to specific answers, therefore warrant further assessment.

Overall, Xiao La Meng is no longer merely a tool for compressing news content. It proactively suggests topics, generates explanations, responds to reader questions, and guides users toward additional coverage. AI now participates at multiple stages of news consumption and information interpretation.

RISK

IN THIS SECTION

Misinterpretation / Oversight / Updates / Accountability

JMSC6140 · FINAL PROJECT

Four places where a reviewed story can become an unreliable answer. Explore the failure, then the safeguard.

EXTERNAL EVIDENCE

The EBU/BBC study highlights problems in accuracy, sourcing and context. Its findings describe external AI assistants—not an error rate for Xiao La Meng.

Study context and findings

4. Key Risks and Dilemmas

In 2025, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and the BBC jointly released the News Integrity in AI Assistants Toolkit, which evaluated more than 3,000 AI responses to news questions across 18 countries and 14 languages. It found that 45% of answers contained major issues that could materially mislead users. The study categorized problems involving factual accuracy, sourcing, contextual completeness, and the distinction between fact and opinion.

These findings suggest that AI news services require more than improvements in technical accuracy: traditional editorial principles must also be extended to every AI-generated response made available to readers.

01Preserve critical conditions

Meaning shifts

A summary can retain the event but lose the conditions that make it true.

THE SAFEGUARDEligibility, chronology, uncertainty and scope must survive the rewrite.

Explore the evidence and editorial standards

1. Risk description

When compressing, reorganizing, and explaining reporting, AI may preserve an event's basic facts while omitting context essential to understanding the story, thereby altering the meaning of the original report.

2. Existing editorial standards

Traditional editorial standards already establish explicit expectations for factual accuracy and contextual completeness.

BBC Editorial Guidelines — Section 3: Accuracy

  • Section 3.4.1 calls for the verification of facts and statistics, identification of important qualifications, and appropriate explanation and contextualization of claims.
  • Section 3.4.19 notes that omitting significant details can make reporting inaccurate and that audiences should receive the relevant facts, complete information, and necessary context: “Omitting significant details may lead to inaccuracy.”
  • Section 3.4.27 recognizes that AI may distort content because of algorithmic bias, training data, hallucinations, and other factors; the BBC must not materially mislead its audiences through any use of AI.

In particular, answering a user's specific question may require AI to extract and recombine information from multiple stories. Even when each source is accurate, the system may mishandle chronology, conditions, statistical scope, or causal relationships during synthesis.

3. Policy requirements

Reviewing the original story does not mean that every subsequent AI response based on it has been fact-checked.

Newsrooms should extend factual-accuracy standards from original reporting to AI-generated news summaries and answers.

AI summaries and answers must preserve the key information that affects factual judgments, including conditions of applicability, temporal context, data limitations, and uncertainty. They must avoid changing a source's meaning through excessive simplification, inaccurate generalization, or confusion between fact and speculation.

02Route by risk

Oversight falls behind

Continuous, personalized answers outgrow article-by-article review.

THE SAFEGUARDMatch human oversight to the consequences of an error.

Explore the evidence and editorial standards

1. Risk description

AI news assistants operate differently. They may respond to readers around the clock, and every user can pose a different question. The traditional article-by-article, prepublication review process cannot simply be applied to every AI answer. This creates two risks:

  • Insufficient human review.
  • Excessive review costs.

2. Existing editorial standards

The BBC expressly treats AI products that distribute or curate news as an editorial experience and requires them to be:

“subject to editorial approval and human oversight.”

Source: BBC, Editorial Guidelines, § 3.4.28.

3. Policy requirements

News organizations therefore need to specify:

  • Which answers may be generated and released through automated processes.
  • Which types of content require human sampling or editorial re-review.
  • Which high-risk questions require human approval before an answer is published.
  • Who has authority to suspend relevant functions when the system behaves abnormally.
03Synchronize corrections

The answer gets old

A genuine source can still support an outdated answer.

THE SAFEGUARDConnect article updates to retrieval, caches and generated responses.

Explore the evidence and editorial standards

1. Risk description

News reporting is not static. As events develop, original articles may be updated, expanded, or corrected, and previously valid information may become obsolete. Yet AI news assistants may continue retrieving older versions of stories, summaries, or cached information, producing answers inconsistent with the latest developments.

2. Existing editorial standards

BBC Editorial Guidelines — Section 3: Accuracy

The BBC establishes explicit provisions for news updates and error correction:

  • Section 3.4.33: Check before publication whether prepared content has been overtaken by subsequent developments.
  • Section 3.4.34: Acknowledge and correct serious factual mistakes promptly, clearly, and appropriately.
  • Section 3.4.35: Correct serious breaches of editorial standards in long-lived or on-demand content promptly and clearly explain the changes made.
  • Section 3.4.36: Correct errors in online news text that could change the editorial meaning and clearly inform audiences that the article has been amended.

3. Policy requirements

Updating or correcting an original article does not mean that related AI-generated content has been corrected at the same time.

Newsrooms should establish a mechanism that synchronizes news updates with AI corrections. When an original report undergoes a significant update or correction, related AI retrieval systems, knowledge bases, caches, and previously generated summaries and answers should be promptly checked and updated to prevent outdated information from being presented to readers.

04Assign editorial ownership

Nobody owns the fix

Responsibility crosses teams; an error can fall between them.

THE SAFEGUARDGive a senior editor clear authority to supervise, correct and suspend.

Explore the evidence and editorial standards

1. Risk description

When an AI news summary or answer contains an error, the problem may involve multiple parties:

The news editorial department; AI product team; technical team; management; and external technology providers.

Without clearly allocated responsibilities, each team may assume that another team is responsible for resolving the issue.

2. Existing editorial standards

BBC Editorial Guidelines — Section 3: Accuracy, § 3.4.27

The BBC provides more specific requirements for accountability in AI applications:

  • A senior editorial figure must take responsibility for and oversee deployment and ongoing use of the AI system.
  • Editorial Policy should be consulted before deploying AI.
  • Significant AI applications affecting audience-facing content should have an identifiable senior editorial owner.

Source: BBC, Editorial Guidelines, § 3.4.27.

3. Policy requirements

News organizations must specify not only how an AI system should operate but also who is authorized to supervise, correct, and suspend the service.

Newsrooms should establish a clear framework of editorial accountability for AI, with a unified reporting and response process that assigns a responsible owner to every AI content issue.

THE COMMON THREAD

Accuracy is a responsibility
across the whole journey.

Explore the policy

POLICY

Designed for trust.
Accountable by people.

IN THIS SECTION

Governance context / Operational rules / Risk tiers

JMSC6140 · FINAL PROJECT

A practical editorial system: preserve the facts, match oversight to risk, and make every correction someone’s responsibility.

Preserve contextAssess riskKeep answers currentOwn the correction
BEFORE & AFTER GENERATION

Shorter answers.
Complete conditions.

Extract a critical-facts checklist before generation. Compare the answer against it; regenerate when conditions, numbers or dates do not match.

Who qualifiesWhen & whereExceptionsData scopeCurrent statusUncertainty
Read the preservation rules

(1) Specify information that must be retained.

Summaries involving policies, public services, statistics, and major events must preserve the affected population, eligibility requirements, time and location, important exceptions, statistical scope, and the event's current status. Context essential to readers' judgments must not be omitted (BBC, n.d., §§ 3.4.1, 3.4.19).

(2) Prohibit misleading simplification.

Do not present exceptional circumstances as universal rules, proposals still under discussion as policies already in force, or predictions, opinions, and unverified claims as established facts (European Broadcasting Union & BBC, 2025).

(3) Establish checks before and after generation.

The system should extract a “critical facts checklist” from the source article and automatically compare eligibility criteria, numbers, and dates against the generated summary. If discrepancies are detected, it should regenerate the output.

RISK-TIERED OVERSIGHT

How much review does an answer need?

Select a tier to see its scope and publication rule.

Verified, stable information

ScopeCultural activities, biographical background and stable historical information.

Release ruleAutomatic responses after source and factual-consistency checks, with periodic human sampling.

Conditions change the answer

ScopeEducation policy, subsidies, complex policies and multi-report synthesis.

Release ruleVerify eligibility, amounts, deadlines and scope. Conflicts, anomalies or complaints trigger editorial review.

Public action is at stake

ScopeMajor disasters, public safety, elections, serious allegations and information affecting public behavior.

Release ruleUse preapproved factual explanations or editor-authorized answers. No definitive conclusion without reliable support.

The highest applicable tier wins. Unverifiable sources, stale information or repeated errors require escalation. A designated editor can suspend the service.

Full oversight policy and sources

Real-time AI answers cannot follow the traditional prepublication editing process one response at a time. News organizations should therefore establish different automatic-release permissions and human-oversight requirements according to the potential consequences of an error (Associated Press, 2026; Poynter Institute, 2025; Chicago Public Media, 2026; BBC, n.d., § 3.4.28).

(1) Low-risk content: Automated checks and periodic sampling.

This tier covers verified cultural activities, biographical background, and stable historical information. AI may respond automatically after source and factual-consistency checks, subject to periodic human sampling.

(2) Medium-risk content: Enhanced verification of facts and conditions.

This tier covers education policy, public-benefit subsidies, complex policies, and syntheses of multiple reports. The system should give particular attention to eligibility, monetary amounts, deadlines, and scope. Conflicting sources, anomalous answers, or user complaints must trigger editorial review.

(3) High-risk content: Prioritize human review.

This tier covers major disasters, public safety, elections, serious allegations, and information that may directly affect public behavior. As a rule, the system should provide only preapproved factual explanations or answers authorized by a designated editor; it must not present definitive conclusions without reliable support.

(4) Establish escalation and suspension procedures.

Where an answer falls into multiple risk tiers, the highest tier applies. Cases involving unverifiable sources, potentially outdated information, or repeated system errors should be escalated automatically, and a designated editor should be authorized to suspend the relevant question-answering functions.

WHEN INFORMATION CHANGES

A correction must travel
as far as the answer.

  1. DetectArticle update, withdrawal or reported error
  2. RepairSource versions, retrieval and cached answers
  3. VerifyRetest the original question with editorial review
  4. ExplainPublic correction; reader notice where feasible and privacy-compliant
Synchronization, timestamps and public corrections

(1) Establish triggers for news updates.

When an original report is substantially corrected, withdrawn, or updated with an important development, the editorial system should transmit the article identifier, type of change, latest version, and update timestamp to the AI service (BBC, n.d., §§ 3.4.33–3.4.36).

(2) Label time-sensitive information.

Information on disasters, transportation, and deadlines for public-service applications should clearly state “as of” what date or time it applies. If currency cannot be confirmed, the system should indicate that verification is underway or suspend definitive answers on the issue.

(3) Establish public corrections and re-verification.

Significant errors already communicated to the public should be accompanied by a correction notice on the relevant answer page. After a technical fix, the original question should be retested. Where privacy requirements are satisfied and users can be contacted, correction notifications may be sent to affected readers (Reuters, n.d.).

HUMAN ACCOUNTABILITY

Shared work.
A clear editorial owner.

External models do not transfer the newsroom’s responsibility for published news.

Senior editorStandards, disputes and suspension decisions

Editorial teamFacts, context, final review and public corrections

Product teamFeedback channels, release rules and escalation

Technical teamRetrieval, logs, version control and cache repair

Ownership, error handling and recordkeeping

(1) Designate an ultimate editorial owner.

The news organization should appoint a senior editor responsible for the editorial standards of the AI news service, resolution of major disputes, and decisions to suspend functions. Even when external AI models are used, the news organization retains ultimate editorial responsibility for news content delivered to the public (BBC, n.d., § 3.4.27; Reuters, n.d.).

(2) Clarify departmental responsibilities.

The editorial department verifies facts and context and manages public corrections; the AI product team maintains user feedback channels, publication rules, and cross-team escalation procedures.

(3) Create a unified error-response workflow.

Each AI answer should offer “View sources” and “Report an error” options. On receiving a report, the duty editor should determine its risk tier, the technical team should investigate and repair the problem, and an editor should then decide whether to resume the service or issue a correction.

(4) Establish recordkeeping and regular evaluation.

The organization should retain the response text, timestamp, source version, and resolution outcome necessary for correcting errors, in line with the principle of data minimization. It should regularly measure omitted critical conditions, unsupported conclusions, recurrence of outdated information, and time to repair errors, and adjust the human-sampling rate in light of pilot findings (Cyberspace Administration of China et al., 2023).

Let questions inform the newsroom.

Use de-identified, aggregated questions to improve answers and reveal reporting gaps. Audience attention cannot replace editorial judgment.

Audience feedback and reporting development

(1) Use audience questions to improve the AI product.

News organizations should regularly analyze frequent questions, repeated follow-ups, and failed answers from Xiao La Meng to identify audience information needs and improve retrieval, response quality, and information presentation. Analysis should prioritize de-identified, aggregated data to protect user privacy (Arguedas, 2026).

(2) Turn audience information needs into reporting leads.

Journalists and editors may use audience questions to identify issues of public concern and gaps in existing coverage, helping generate ideas for policy explainers, in-depth features, and follow-up reporting. However, audience attention must not replace independent editorial judgments about newsworthiness and the public interest (Adami, 2026).

THE GOVERNANCE CONTEXT

The framework behind the rules

Applicability depends on the service. Historical integrations do not establish the assistant’s current model.

Chinese regulatory context and limits

China's existing AI governance framework provides an important policy context for this project. The Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services took effect on August 15, 2023. They call on providers of generative AI services to improve the accuracy, reliability, and transparency of generated content according to the nature and characteristics of their services, and to establish complaint and reporting mechanisms. Importantly, the measures also delimit their scope and state that where other provisions govern activities such as news publishing, those provisions apply. Accordingly, this project does not assume that every provision automatically applies to all internal Hunan Daily workflows; applicability must be considered in light of the nature of the service and its use cases.

The Measures for Labeling AI-Generated and Synthetic Content, released in March 2025 and effective September 1 of that year, further clarify labeling obligations. They distinguish between explicit and implicit labels and require AI-generated or synthetic content to be marked as prescribed by relevant rules.

At present, Xiao La Meng displays “Content generated by AI; for reference only” beneath its AI-generated responses. The notice helps readers understand how the content was produced and illustrates the importance of transparency. However, labeling AI content does not constitute fact-checking and does not establish that human editorial review took place. Even where readers know that a passage was generated by AI, the news organization still needs to ensure its factual, statistical, and contextual accuracy.

On May 8, 2026, the Cyberspace Administration of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology issued the Implementation Opinions on the Standardized Application and Innovative Development of AI Agents. The document calls for clear decision-making authority for agents, stronger risk monitoring and safety management, tiered governance, and enhanced human–AI collaborative review. These principles offer further guidance for news organizations managing AI news services.

We have not, however, obtained sufficient technical documentation to confirm whether every feature of Xiao La Meng falls within the document's definition of an AI agent. We therefore use its principles of risk management, human–AI collaboration, and allocation of responsibilities as governance references rather than assuming that Xiao La Meng necessarily falls within a particular regulated category.

Technology providers and responsibility

As news organizations increasingly depend on external models and technology platforms, an AI service may involve multiple parties, including the newsroom, model developers, and technology service providers. News organizations therefore need to understand which parts of the service they control and which depend on external suppliers.

In February 2025, Hunan Daily publicly reported that the New Hunan app and its editorial platform had integrated DeepSeek-R1, upgrading Xiao La Meng's capabilities. This historical report establishes that DeepSeek played a role in the development of New Hunan's AI features at that time. It does not, however, prove that all functions of New Hunan 13.0 in 2026 still use the same model or deployment arrangement. We therefore do not identify DeepSeek as Xiao La Meng's sole or current underlying model provider.

Nevertheless, DeepSeek's publicly available terms of service provide a reference point for understanding how AI technology providers allocate responsibility. Under the DeepSeek Open Platform Terms of Service, effective April 29, 2026, DeepSeek primarily provides foundational model services, while parties building and operating downstream applications also bear responsibility for those applications and their corresponding legal obligations. The terms also cover data security, risk monitoring, alerts, and emergency response.

DeepSeek's privacy policy, updated in February 2026, also indicates that its consumer-facing privacy policy does not automatically cover all data processing carried out by downstream applications developed through the Open Platform. Developers and operators of those applications must disclose their data-handling practices as appropriate.

These provisions reveal a key issue: technical responsibility for AI services may be distributed among multiple parties, and not every failure can simply be attributed to the model. News organizations need to understand what external providers supply, how user inputs are handled, and how updates to models or systems may affect news content.

EFFECT

Start small.
Measure what matters.

IN THIS SECTION

12-week pilot / Six evaluation dimensions / Continuing review

JMSC6140 · FINAL PROJECT

Test the framework in a 12-week pilot. Measure whether the newsroom can find, explain and repair misleading answers—not promise that AI never makes mistakes.

PROPOSED PILOT · NO RESULTS YET

Start with Hunan Daily-based summaries, suggested questions, article Q&A and related recommendations. Internal AI applications remain outside the initial scope.

12 WEEKS / THREE PHASES

Start with evidence.
Refine in practice.

Select a phase to explore its work and expected outputs.

PHASE 1

Establish baseline

Editorial, product, and technical teams review current workflows. Select approximately 50 reports on health, policy, technology, and social affairs; test article summaries, suggested questions, article Q&A, and related-news recommendations; record source versions, prompts, outputs, and human assessments.

Expected outputs

Baseline data, risk inventory, confirmed responsibilities, and a sample of high-risk outputs.

PHASE 2

Policy pilot

Implement the source and context checks, three-tier risk routing, version synchronization, and error reporting described in Section 6. Prioritize key news categories and monitor human workload.

Expected outputs

Review and escalation logs, correction cases, system adjustments, and editorial feedback.

PHASE 3

Evaluate and refine

Compare results against baseline; analyze recurring errors, risk-routing accuracy, correction speed, source verifiability, and review costs; revise rules and decide whether to expand coverage.

Expected outputs

Internal assessment report, revised policy, and recommendations for scaling up.

WHAT TO MEASURE

Six signals of editorial integrity.

Expand a measure to see how it would be assessed. These are proposed measures, not performance claims.

Factual accuracy

MeasureShare of tested outputs with factual errors confirmed by human reviewers.

Why it mattersAssess consistency between outputs and sources.

Preservation of critical context

MeasureShare of required eligibility, timing, scope, exception, and other conditions retained correctly.

Why it mattersIdentify oversimplification and misleading summaries.

Source traceability

MeasureShare of answers whose key factual claims can be linked to clearly supporting evidence.

Why it mattersAssess readers’ ability to verify answers.

Quality of related-news recommendations

MeasureShare of recommended articles judged by human reviewers to be relevant to the question.

Why it mattersEvaluate whether further reading is useful.

Effectiveness of risk tiering

MeasureShare of high-risk outputs found through sampling that should have been escalated but were not.

Why it mattersAssess risk routing and human oversight.

Correction efficiency and review burden

MeasureTime from confirmed error to completed fix; average time spent on human review.

Why it mattersAssess timeliness and operational sustainability.

New model. New retrieval.
Test the risks again.

Repeat relevant tests after major changes to the model, retrieval, recommendation logic or user interactions.

Complete implementation plan and evaluation framework

7. Policy Implementation and Evaluation

We recommend a 12-week pilot in the New Hunan app, initially covering article summaries, suggested questions, article-based Q&A, and related-news recommendations grounded in Hunan Daily's published content. The first phase should not encompass every internal AI application used by the organization.

7.1 Three-Phase Pilot Plan

PeriodMain activitiesExpected outputs
Weeks 1–2: Establish baselineEditorial, product, and technical teams review current workflows. Select approximately 50 reports on health, policy, technology, and social affairs; test article summaries, suggested questions, article Q&A, and related-news recommendations; record source versions, prompts, outputs, and human assessments.Baseline data, risk inventory, confirmed responsibilities, and a sample of high-risk outputs.
Weeks 3–8: Policy pilotImplement the source and context checks, three-tier risk routing, version synchronization, and error reporting described in Section 6. Prioritize key news categories and monitor human workload.Review and escalation logs, correction cases, system adjustments, and editorial feedback.
Weeks 9–12: Evaluate and refineCompare results against baseline; analyze recurring errors, risk-routing accuracy, correction speed, source verifiability, and review costs; revise rules and decide whether to expand coverage.Internal assessment report, revised policy, and recommendations for scaling up.

7.2 Implementation Responsibilities and Escalation Authority

A senior editor should lead the working group. The editorial department retains final judgment over factual accuracy, context, and public corrections; the product team coordinates workflows and ensures that feedback channels function; and the technical team implements retrieval, logs, version control, and cache repairs. These responsibilities should follow Section 6.4 rather than creating a second, potentially contradictory accountability structure.

7.3 Evaluation Metrics

Evaluation dimensionSuggested measurementPurpose
Factual accuracyShare of tested outputs with factual errors confirmed by human reviewers.Assess consistency between outputs and sources.
Preservation of critical contextShare of required eligibility, timing, scope, exception, and other conditions retained correctly.Identify oversimplification and misleading summaries.
Source traceabilityShare of answers whose key factual claims can be linked to clearly supporting evidence.Assess readers’ ability to verify answers.
Quality of related-news recommendationsShare of recommended articles judged by human reviewers to be relevant to the question.Evaluate whether further reading is useful.
Effectiveness of risk tieringShare of high-risk outputs found through sampling that should have been escalated but were not.Assess risk routing and human oversight.
Correction efficiency and review burdenTime from confirmed error to completed fix; average time spent on human review.Assess timeliness and operational sustainability.

7.4 Continuing Review

An internal report should be produced at the end of the 12-week pilot. Relevant risk tests should then be repeated whenever major changes are made to the underlying model, news retrieval system, recommendation logic, or user-facing interactions. The policy should not be judged solely by whether AI “never makes mistakes,” but by whether the news organization can promptly detect, explain, and correct outputs that could mislead the public.
